newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hogs seen below year ago, but set to increase.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hogs seen below year ago, but set to increase.

text.p: CHICAGO, Dec 24, Reuter - The number of hogs on U.S. farms is seen slightly below last year after liquidation earlier in the year, but expansion is now under way, analysts said.
The trend is expected to be confirmed by Friday's U.S. Agriculture Department Hogs and Pigs Report.

"The industry is on an expansion track. There was more than a 14 percent drop in sow and boar slaughter during the period and almost a nine percent increase in the retention of gilts to go into the breeding herd compared to last year," said Chuck Levitt, livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
USDA's data will be released Friday at 1400 CST/2000 GMT.

Analysts' estimates for all hogs and pigs on U.S. farms as of December 1 averaged 98.4 percent of a year ago and ranged from 95.0 to 101.0 percent. Estimates on hogs kept for breeding averaged 101.6 percent in a range of 99.9 to 104.0 percent and hogs kept for marketing averaged 97.5 percent of a year ago in a range of 94.0 to 99.0 percent.

Levitt noted that the September 1 Hogs and Pigs report showed the breeding herd down two percent from the previous year. However, three months later, Levitt said he expects the breeding herd is up two percent from a year ago.
"The breeding herd has had one of the most significant expansions that we have seen in several years," he said.
Levitt, who estimated all hogs at 99.2 percent of a year ago, said the large hog producers were getting back up to speed after cutting back last spring.
He also noted the moderate-sized Midwest hog growers were expanding because it was more profitable to them to feed corn to hogs than to sell it.
Nearby Chicago Board of Trade corn prices have more than halved from a peak in excess of $5.50 a bushel in early July to a current price of about $2.65 a bushel.

Some analysts believe the expansion of hog herds started in the fall while others believe it only kicked into gear just recently, with University of Missouri economist Ron Plain holding the latter opinion.

Plain said he disagrees with the USDA September report on farrowing intentions which were originally estimated at even with last year. For that to have happened, the expansion of the hog herd would have to have started back when corn was at $5 per bushel, he noted.
Also, hog numbers are much lower than the USDA has been reporting, he said.

"The USDA has failed to get their numbers low enough in the last four reports. Slaughters continue to come in below what has been indicated and I think they need to revise down their numbers," Plain said.
Plain put all hogs at 95 percent of a year ago.
But he agrees with most other analysts that expansion of the hog herd is now underway.

Since September 1 there has been a rapid increase which can be seen by farrowings rising from 94 percent in September/November to projections at 102 percent in December/February and 106 percent for March/May, Plain said.
